title: Segment Tree for Range Sum
directAnswer: When you must both query a range sum and update single elements many times, a plain array forces one of the two operations to be O(n). A segment tree stores partial sums in a binary tree: each node owns a sub-interval and holds the sum of that interval. Build is O(n), a range-sum query is O(log n), and a point update is O(log n). Store the tree in a flat array of size about 4n; the children of node i sit at 2i and 2i+1.

remember.pattern: Recursive interval tree: each node holds the aggregate of its sub-range
remember.formula:
build(node, lo, hi):
    if lo == hi: tree[node] = a[lo]; return
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    build(2*node, lo, mid); build(2*node+1, mid+1, hi)
    tree[node] = tree[2*node] + tree[2*node+1]
rules: Allocate the tree array with size **4n** — a safe upper bound that avoids index overflow for any n.
Each node covers **[lo, hi]**; recurse into the half (or halves) that overlap the query range.
A query node returns **0** (the additive identity) when its range is fully outside the query — never recurse further there.
A point update changes **one leaf**, then re-sums each ancestor on the way back up — that is the O(log n).
The merge for sum is `+`; swap it for `min`, `max`, or `gcd` and the same structure handles those queries.
whenToUse: Many interleaved range queries AND point/range updates on the same array
Aggregates that compose associatively: sum, min, max, gcd, xor
Online queries where you cannot precompute all answers up front
When prefix sums break because the array keeps changing
antiSignals: Array is static (no updates) → a prefix-sum array gives O(1) queries with no tree
Only point updates + prefix-sum queries → a Fenwick (BIT) tree is shorter to write
Aggregate is not associative (e.g. 'most frequent element') → segment tree merge breaks down
n is tiny and queries are few → a plain loop is simpler and fast enough
remember.takeaway: A segment tree buys balance: instead of fast-query/slow-update or slow-query/fast-update, both become O(log n). The whole idea is that any range decomposes into O(log n) precomputed canonical intervals, so you merge a handful of stored partials instead of scanning.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize that interleaved updates and range queries rule out prefix sums, and whether you can implement the three-way overlap logic (no overlap / total overlap / partial overlap) correctly.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Returning the wrong identity for the 'no overlap' case (e.g. returning a stored value instead of 0), or under-sizing the tree array to 2n and overflowing, or forgetting to re-sum ancestors after an update.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Start with the array baseline and state the O(n) cost of one operation, then explain that a range decomposes into O(log n) canonical nodes. Mention that swapping `+` for `min`/`max` reuses the entire structure.

problemStatement:
Design a data structure over an integer array `a[0..n-1]` that supports two operations efficiently after building:

1. ***rangeSum(l, r)*** — return the sum of `a[l] + a[l+1] + … + a[r]`.
2. ***update(i, val)*** — set `a[i] = val`.

The operations are interleaved and there can be up to 10⁵ of each. Build once, then answer every operation in ***O(log n)***.
constraints: Up to 10⁵ mixed update and rangeSum calls
0 ≤ l ≤ r ≤ n − 1 for every query
Values fit in 64-bit after summation (use long in Java)
understanding: We need a structure where neither operation degrades to O(n). The key realization: a sum over any range can be assembled from a small set of precomputed interval sums. A segment tree precomputes the sum of every 'canonical' interval (the whole array, each half, each quarter, …) so any query range is covered by O(log n) of them, and any single value change touches only O(log n) of them.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are updates point updates or range updates?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Point updates here (set one index). Range updates need lazy propagation, which is a layer on top of this same tree — worth mentioning as the follow-up.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the array static or changing?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Changing. If it were static, a prefix-sum array gives O(1) queries and no tree is needed — say that to show you reach for the simplest tool first.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What aggregate — sum, min, max?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Sum here, but the structure is identical for any associative merge. Only the combine step and the identity element change.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the recursion get deep enough to overflow the stack?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Depth is O(log n) ≈ 17 for n = 10⁵, so recursion is safe. For pedagogically deep structures you would switch to the iterative bottom-up segment tree, which I can mention.

approaches.name: Baseline — Plain Array (Loop the Range)
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first: it is correct and trivial, and it makes the cost trade-off obvious before you reach for a tree.
hints: Store the array as-is. update(i, val) is a single assignment — O(1).
rangeSum(l, r) loops from l to r adding each element — O(n) per query.
With up to 10⁵ queries each scanning up to 10⁵ elements, that is up to 10¹⁰ operations. Too slow — this motivates the tree.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Update writes one cell (O(1)). A query sums up to n cells (O(n)). With q queries the total is O(q·n), which blows up when both q and n are large.
approaches.explanation:
The simplest correct structure is the array itself.

**Update is trivial.** Setting `a[i] = val` is one assignment, O(1). Nothing else to maintain.

**Query is a loop.** To answer `rangeSum(l, r)` you add `a[l]` through `a[r]` directly — up to n additions in the worst case.

**Why this is not enough.** The problem allows up to 10⁵ queries, each potentially spanning the whole array. That is up to 10¹⁰ additions — far beyond what runs in time. The opposite extreme, a prefix-sum array, flips the trade: queries become O(1) but every update forces you to rebuild the suffix of the prefix array, again O(n). Neither extreme is good when updates and queries are interleaved.

**The lesson that points to the tree.** We want *both* operations sub-linear. The segment tree achieves O(log n) for each by storing partial sums at multiple granularities, so neither a query nor an update ever touches more than O(log n) of them.
approaches.insight: The array baseline and the prefix-sum array are the two endpoints of a trade: one makes updates cheap and queries expensive, the other does the reverse. The segment tree sits in the middle, paying a logarithm for both — which is exactly what you want when neither operation is rare.

approaches.name: Segment Tree — Recursive Array Implementation (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want once updates and queries are interleaved. 'Each node owns an interval and stores its sum; both operations walk O(log n) nodes.'

complexity.time: O(n) build, O(log n) query, O(log n) update

hints: Build a binary tree where each node owns a contiguous sub-interval and stores the sum of that interval. The root owns [0, n-1].
For a query, classify each node three ways: its interval is fully outside the query (return 0), fully inside (return its stored sum), or partially overlapping (recurse into both children and add).
For an update, walk down to the single leaf for index i, set it, then re-sum each ancestor on the way back up. Store the tree in a flat array of size 4n; children of node v are 2v and 2v+1.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Build visits each of the O(n) tree nodes once → O(n). A query or update descends from the root; at each level it follows at most a constant number of partially-overlapping nodes, and the tree height is O(log n) → O(log n) per operation. The flat tree array uses O(n) space (4n is the safe bound).
approaches.explanation:
A segment tree is a balanced binary tree laid over the array. The root represents the whole range `[0, n-1]`; each internal node splits its range at the midpoint into a left child `[lo, mid]` and a right child `[mid+1, hi]`; the leaves are the individual elements. Every node stores the sum of its own interval.

**Why any query is O(log n).** The central fact is that *any* sub-range `[l, r]` can be written as the disjoint union of O(log n) of these canonical intervals. When the query descends from the root, at each node one of three things happens: the node's interval is completely outside `[l, r]` (contribute the identity, 0, and stop), completely inside `[l, r]` (return the node's stored sum and stop — no need to go deeper), or it partially overlaps (recurse into both children and add the results). Only the partial-overlap nodes branch, and there are at most O(log n) of those along each side of the range, so the query touches O(log n) nodes total.

**Why the identity matters.** For a sum, the 'fully outside' case must contribute `0` — the additive identity — so it changes nothing. If the aggregate were `min`, the identity would be `+∞`; for `max` it would be `−∞`. Returning a stored value or the wrong identity here is the classic bug that silently corrupts answers.

**Why any update is O(log n).** Changing `a[i]` affects exactly the chain of nodes whose intervals contain `i` — that is one node per level, from the leaf up to the root, O(log n) of them. We set the leaf to the new value, then on the way back up recompute each parent as the sum of its two children. Every other node is untouched because its interval does not contain `i`.

**Why build is O(n).** Building fills each node's sum once in a post-order pass: a leaf copies its array element, an internal node adds its two children. There are about 2n nodes, so the build is linear.

**Why a flat array of size 4n.** Storing the tree implicitly (node `v` has children `2v` and `2v+1`, starting the root at index 1) avoids pointers entirely. When n is not a power of two the recursion can reach indices up to slightly below 4n, so 4n is the safe allocation that never overflows.
approaches.insight: The engine is interval decomposition: precompute the sum of a logarithmic set of nested intervals, and then every range is a union of O(log n) of them while every element belongs to only O(log n) of them. That symmetry — few intervals cover a range, few intervals contain a point — is what makes *both* query and update logarithmic. Swap the `+` merge and the `0` identity for `min`/`+∞` or `max`/`−∞` and the identical code answers range-min or range-max.

Internal node = sum of its two children; used in both build and update.
No overlap with the query — return the identity 0 and stop descending.

java.line: return tree[node];        // fully inside: stored sum
java.explanation: Total overlap — use the precomputed sum without recursing further. This is why queries are O(log n).

java.line: update(2 * node, lo, mid, i, val);
java.explanation: Descend only into the child whose interval contains i — one path, O(log n).

edgeCases.behavior: Tree is a single leaf at the root; both query and update touch one node. The 4n allocation still works.
Whole-array query stops at the root in O(1) because the root's interval is fully inside.
Sums work unchanged; use 64-bit (long) so large totals do not overflow.

pitfalls: Allocating only 2n for the tree array — overflows when n is not a power of two; use 4n.
Returning the wrong identity in the no-overlap case (anything but 0 for sum) — silently wrong answers.
Forgetting to re-sum ancestors after an update — stale sums above the changed leaf.
Using int for the sum in Java when totals can exceed 2³¹ — overflow; use long.

commonMistakes: Under-sizing the tree array to 2n and overflowing on non-power-of-two n.
Returning a stored value instead of the identity (0) for the no-overlap case.
Forgetting to recompute ancestor sums after a point update.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Tree array too small
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When n is not a power of two, the recursion reaches node indices above 2n. Allocating 2n overflows the array; 4n is the safe bound that always fits.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: tree = new long[2 * n];   // index out of bounds for many n
commonMistakesDetailed.good: tree = new long[4 * n];   // safe for any n

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong identity for no-overlap
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When a node's interval is fully outside the query, it must contribute the additive identity 0 so it changes nothing. Returning a stored sum or a sentinel corrupts the merged result.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if r < lo or hi < l:
    return self.tree[node]   # wrong: pollutes the sum
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if r < lo or hi < l:
    return 0                 # additive identity

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Not re-summing ancestors on update
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A point update changes a leaf but every ancestor's stored sum also depended on it. If you set the leaf and return, all the sums above it are stale.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
# ... recurse into the correct child, then:
    self.tree[node] = self.tree[2 * node] + self.tree[2 * node + 1]

patternNote: Segment tree: store an associative aggregate over every canonical interval so any range is a union of O(log n) nodes and any element belongs to O(log n) nodes. Reach for it when point/range updates and range queries are interleaved. Swap the merge (+, min, max, gcd) and its identity to handle other aggregates.
